Meta.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Open Science in AI: A Replication Study
Meta.venue: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)

hypothesis_1.hypothesis: The authors hypothesise that the availability of both code and data significantly increases the reproducibility of AI research compared to studies where only data is shared.
hypothesis_1.reason: The hypothesis is implied in the abstract, introduction, and results sections. The authors state that '86% of articles that shared code and data were fully or partly reproduced, while this was true for 33% of articles that shared only data.' This is further supported in the discussion and conclusion, where they emphasize the importance of open science and sharing both code and data for reproducibility.

hypothesis_2.hypothesis: The authors hypothesise that the quality of data documentation is more strongly correlated with successful replication than the quality of code documentation in AI research.
hypothesis_2.reason: This is implied in the abstract and results sections, where the authors state: 'The quality of the data documentation correlates with successful replication. Poorly documented or miss-specified data will probably result in unsuccessful replication. Surprisingly, the quality of the code documentation does not correlate with successful replication.'

experiment_1.experiment_description: A systematic replication study of 30 highly cited AI articles, attempting to reproduce their results based on the availability of code and data. The study classified articles into R3 (only data shared) and R4 (both code and data shared) reproducibility types and measured the success rate of replication for each type.
metrics: Reproducibility success rate (Success, Partial Success, Failure, No Result)
Percentage of experiments with identical, consistent, or failed results
experiment_1.statistics: Descriptive statistics (percentages, counts) and logistic regression analysis to identify problem types correlated with irreproducibility.
data: Publicly available code and data from original studies (This work)
experiment_1.test: Comparison of success rates between R3 and R4 studies using descriptive statistics and logistic regression to identify significant problem types (e.g., P15, P7, P18).
experiment_1.strategy: Replication of experiments as described in the original articles, with a time limit of 40 hours per study. Studies were classified based on the availability of code and data, and results were aggregated to determine overall reproducibility.

interpretation_1.reason: The results strongly support the hypothesis. The study found that 86% of R4 studies (code and data shared) were successfully or partially reproduced, compared to only 33% of R3 studies (only data shared). The authors conclude that 'sharing both code and data increases the chance of reproducing results immensely' (p. 10).

interpretation_2.reason: The results support the hypothesis. The study identified that problems related to data documentation (e.g., P15, P18) were among the most significant predictors of irreproducibility, while issues with code documentation were less impactful. The authors state: 'The quality of the data documentation correlates with successful replication. Poorly documented or miss-specified data will probably result in unsuccessful replication. Surprisingly, the quality of the code documentation does not correlate with successful replication' (p. 1).
